---
title: "3.1 Digital Voltage Levels and Logic States"
description: "Interpret high, low, indeterminate, and unsafe GPIO voltages before connecting a switch or sensor."
sidebar: tej
toc: true
execute: {enabled: false}
---

Digital inputs measure voltage. The input circuit compares the pin voltage with thresholds specified by the device manufacturer.

| Region | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| $V_{IN}\leq V_{IL(\max)}$ | guaranteed low |
| $V_{IL(\max)}<V_{IN}<V_{IH(\min)}$ | not guaranteed |
| $V_{IN}\geq V_{IH(\min)}$ | guaranteed high, provided the voltage remains within absolute limits |

## Compatibility check

1. Identify the receiving device supply and GPIO domain.
2. Find guaranteed input-high and input-low thresholds.
3. Check absolute maximum pin voltage.
4. Check whether the source remains valid while the receiving device is unpowered.
5. Select an approved direct connection, divider, buffer, or level shifter.

Raspberry Pi documentation describes its general-purpose header pins as 3.3 V GPIO and warns against using 5 V for 3.3 V components. A nearby 5 V power pin does not make an input 5 V tolerant. See the official [Raspberry Pi GPIO documentation](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html#gpio-and-the-40-pin-header).

::: {.callout-warning title="Hardware boundary"}
Check the exact board and processor. Do not generalize one Arduino, Raspberry Pi, micro:bit, or other microcontroller specification to another device.
:::
